chapters.title: Chapter 6: When to Hedge and When Not To

lessons.title: Building Your Personal Hedging Plan: A Worked Example

children.text: Every mistake in the previous lesson has the same root: decisions made while the market is moving. The cure is unglamorous. Write the plan down in a calm week, in plain language, with numbers, and then follow it. This final lesson gives you a nine-line template, fills it in completely for one investor, tests the result against a crash, and then shows the equally valid plan of an investor whose conclusion is not to hedge at all. By the end you will have everything you need to write your own on a single page.

body.text: A hedging plan is not a market view. It is a set of rules, written before the market moves, that tells you what you are protecting, how much you will spend, what you will buy, and when you will stop.

body.caption: Every line needs a number or a rule, not an opinion

cells: Which rupees am I protecting, and by when?
How far can the portfolio fall and still fund the goal?
What is my beta-weighted Nifty exposure, and how reliable is it?
Under what conditions do I hedge at all?
Which contract, which strike, which expiry?
How many lots, and how do I round?
What is the most I will spend per year?
When do I close, roll or recalculate?
What will I never do, whatever the market does?

children.text: Shalini, 59, is a college professor in Coimbatore who retires in eight months. She has ₹55 lakh in equity funds and ₹20 lakh already in PPF and debt funds. At retirement she will move ₹45 lakh of the equity into a mix of the Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme and short-duration debt funds to fund her first decade. The Nifty is at 25,000 and India VIX is 12.

body.caption: Shalini's equity portfolio and its Nifty-equivalent exposure

stats.label: Exact lots for a full hedge

body.title: Check her lot count
body.prompt: Shalini's beta-weighted exposure is ₹55,00,000. The Nifty is at 25,000 and the lot size is 65. How many lots would a 100% hedge require? (Two decimal places.)
body.explanation: Notional per lot = 25,000 × 65 = ₹16,25,000. Lots = 55,00,000 ÷ 16,25,000 = 3.38. She can buy 3 lots, about 89% hedged, or 4 lots, about 118% hedged and therefore partly a bet on a fall.

cells: Protect the ₹45 lakh I must move to debt at retirement in eight months. Nothing else.
18.2%. Below that, my retirement income plan does not work.
₹55 lakh portfolio, beta-weighted exposure ₹55 lakh. Mid cap fund has R-squared of 0.70, so I will allow a buffer for basis risk.
Hedge now, because the goal is inside twelve months and India VIX is 12, which is cheap. If VIX had been above 20 I would have moved part of the money to debt early instead.
Nifty puts, 23,500 strike (6% below), quarterly expiry, rolled once so that cover runs past my retirement date.
3 lots, 195 units, about 89% of exposure. Rounding down because the premium saved matters more than the last 11%, and my worst case still clears ₹45 lakh.
Maximum 1.5% of the portfolio, about ₹82,500, for the whole eight months.
Close the hedge the day I move ₹45 lakh to debt. Recalculate lots at the roll and after any 10% Nifty move. If a payoff arrives, set aside a third for tax immediately.
No extra lots on market views. No weekly options. No selling options. No closing the hedge because it has lost value.

body.text: Notice line 4. The plan does not say "hedge when the market looks risky". It names a condition, a goal inside twelve months, and a price test, India VIX at 12. It also states the alternative she would have used if protection had been expensive. That is what makes a plan useful in a panic: the decision was already made, by a calmer version of her.

children.text: Testing the Plan Before Using It

A plan is only worth writing if it survives the scenario that worries you. Shalini's portfolio behaves like 220 Nifty units (₹55,00,000 ÷ 25,000). Her three lots cover 195 of them. The 23,500 put costs ₹165 per unit, so ₹32,175 for one quarter. Here is where she lands at expiry, against the ₹45 lakh she must have.

body.caption: Shalini's equity at expiry, unhedged and with 3 lots of the 23,500 put (illustrative)

body.title: Shalini's equity at expiry against her ₹45 lakh requirement

children.text: The unhedged line cuts below her requirement at about an 18% fall. The hedged line never does, even at Nifty 17,500. The hedge costs her about ₹32,000 a quarter, or roughly 0.6% of the portfolio, and in exchange her retirement plan works in every column of the table. That is what a well-specified hedge looks like: boring, cheap, and decisive exactly where it matters.

body.text: One honest caveat, and her plan names it. Her mid cap fund has an R-squared of 0.70, so in a sharp sell-off her portfolio could fall more than beta predicts, and 11% of her exposure is unhedged anyway. In the 30% column she has roughly ₹4.9 lakh of headroom above her goal, which is her real buffer against that basis risk. If the mid cap fund were half her portfolio rather than 15%, that headroom would not be enough, and the answer would be to reduce the mid cap holding rather than buy more puts.

body.title: Which line does the work?
body.question: Six months into her plan, the Nifty has risen to 27,000 and a friend tells Shalini that markets look overheated and she should double her puts. Which line of her plan settles the question?
body.explanation: Line 9 says no extra lots on market views. Doubling the puts would take her well above her exposure, turning the hedge into a short position. She should, however, recalculate her lot count under line 8, because a Nifty move above 10% changes the notional value per lot.

body.title: The point of writing it down
body.textWithBlank: A hedging plan should be written when markets are ___, because that is the only time you can think clearly about them.
body.explanation: Every expensive mistake in the previous lesson, late hedging, over-hedging and abandonment, is a decision made under stress. Writing the rules in a quiet week is what removes them.

children.text: The Other Valid Plan: Aarti's One-Liner

Aarti, 29, has ₹8 lakh in index funds, a ₹30,000 monthly SIP and no goal for twenty years. Her plan is three lines long, and it is complete: my portfolio is below one lot of exposure, so options cannot hedge it; falls make my SIP cheaper, so I do not want them to stop; therefore I will not hedge, and I will not stop or reduce my SIP in any drawdown, including one of 40% or more. She has written the second half precisely because that is the decision she might otherwise get wrong.

columns.label: Shalini, 59, retiring in 8 months
points: Large corpus, no future contributions, hard deadline
Tolerable drawdown 18.2%, which a normal correction could breach
Hedges 89% of exposure with 23,500 puts, budget 1.5% for eight months
Closes the hedge the day the money moves to debt
Main risk: basis risk from her mid cap fund

columns.label: Aarti, 29, no goal for 20 years
points: Small corpus, large future SIPs, no deadline
No hedge, because one lot would cover more than twice her portfolio
Written commitment to keep the SIP running in any crash
Main risk: her own behaviour, not the market

body.title: Write the plan for Ganesh
body.scenario: Ganesh, 46, is a mechanical engineer in Chennai. He has ₹38 lakh in equity funds: ₹26 lakh in a Nifty 50 index fund, ₹8 lakh in a large cap fund with a beta of 0.95, and ₹4 lakh in a small cap fund with a beta of 0.8 and an R-squared of 0.45. His SIP is ₹40,000 a month. His daughter starts an engineering degree in 14 months and he will need ₹14 lakh for the first two years. The Nifty is at 25,000 and India VIX is 11.
body.prompt: Write the nine-line plan you would recommend for Ganesh, with numbers.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Purpose: protect the ₹14 lakh needed in 14 months for the first two years of fees. The rest is long-term money.
2. Tolerable drawdown: 1 − 14 ÷ 38 = 63%. Almost no realistic market fall threatens this goal, which is the single most important finding.
3. Exposure: beta-weighted exposure = 26 + (8 × 0.95) + (4 × 0.8) = ₹36.8 lakh, portfolio beta about 0.97. The small cap fund's R-squared of 0.45 makes part of that unreliable.
4. Trigger: none for now. Because the tolerable drawdown is so wide, no hedge is justified. Revisit if he decides to earmark a much larger sum, or if the fee requirement rises sharply.
5. Instrument and strike: not applicable while no hedge is triggered. If one were needed later, Nifty puts about 6% below the market, quarterly expiry.
6. Size: not applicable. For reference, a full hedge would be 36.8 ÷ 16.25 = 2.26 lots.
7. Budget: zero this year. If a hedge is ever triggered, cap it at 1% of the portfolio a year.
8. Exit and review: review at the annual portfolio check and whenever the fee requirement or timeline changes. Twelve months before the money is needed, move ₹14 lakh in stages into a short-duration debt fund, which removes the goal risk entirely at no premium.
9. Prohibitions: no hedging on market views, no weekly options, no reduction in the SIP during a fall.
The substance of the plan is the staged move to debt, not any option. That is the right answer far more often than this course's subject matter might suggest.

body.title: When the plan and your gut disagree

children.text: It will happen. The market will fall, your hedge will look inadequate, and every instinct will say do something. Three rules help:
Read the plan before acting, especially line 9. Most urges are already covered by something you wrote.

Separate a change in facts from a change in feelings. A redemption, a new goal or a 10% index move are facts, and the plan tells you to recalculate. A frightening headline is not a fact about your portfolio.

If you still want to change the plan, change it in writing, dated, with the reason. Six months later you will be able to see whether you were thinking or reacting, which is the only way anyone improves at this.

body.label: The most common correct plan
body.context: For investors with long horizons, growing SIPs and no near-term goals, the plan is a decision not to hedge plus a commitment not to panic. That is still a plan, and writing it is what makes it hold.

body.title: Write your own plan this week
steps: List every goal needing money from your equity portfolio in the next three years, with rupee amounts and dates, and calculate the tolerable drawdown for the nearest one.
Calculate your beta-weighted Nifty exposure and note the R-squared of every holding, flagging anything below 0.80.
Decide your trigger: the conditions under which you would hedge, including a maximum India VIX level, and the alternative you would use instead if protection is expensive.
If a hedge is triggered, write the strike rule, expiry rule, lot count, rounding decision and annual budget as percentages and rupees.
Write the exit rule, the review triggers and a short list of prohibitions, then save the page somewhere you will actually find it during a crash.

body.label: NSE Option Chain
body.description: The one page you will return to whenever your plan tells you to price a hedge: strikes, premiums and implied volatility for the expiry you need.

cards.definition: A written set of rules covering purpose, tolerable drawdown, exposure, trigger, instrument, size, budget, exit and prohibitions.
The stated conditions under which you will hedge, such as a goal within twelve months and India VIX below a set level.
The maximum you will spend on protection in a year, as a percentage of the portfolio.
An event that forces recalculation: a roll, a 10% index move, a redemption or a change in goals.
The things you commit never to do, such as adding lots on a market view or selling naked options.
The gap between your hedged worst case and the amount your goal needs. Your real buffer against basis risk.

points: A hedging plan has nine lines: purpose, tolerable drawdown, exposure, trigger, instrument and strike, size, budget, exit and review, and prohibitions.
Write it in a calm market. Every expensive mistake comes from deciding while prices are moving.
Test the plan against a severe fall before using it, and check that the hedged outcome still clears the amount your goal needs.
Headroom above the goal is your buffer against basis risk. If a low R-squared holding is large, fix the holding rather than buying more puts.
Deciding not to hedge is a complete plan, and for long-horizon investors with SIPs it is usually the right one.
Review on facts, not feelings: rolls, 10% index moves, redemptions and changed goals. Change the plan only in writing.

body.text: You have reached the end of the course. The most valuable thing you now own is not a strategy. It is the ability to say exactly what you are protecting, what it costs, and whether it is worth it.

This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The plans, portfolios, premiums and outcomes shown are illustrative examples, not recommendations, and real option prices and market outcomes will differ. Options carry risk, and SEBI's own data shows most individual F&O participants lose money. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before building or acting on a hedging plan, and a tax professional about the treatment of any options position.
